turns.question: I calibrate the oxygen sensor in air at the truck and then the pod goes into brackish water. What do I actually have to have right at the truck for that calibration to mean anything once it's in the water?
turns.answer:
For an air calibration to carry over into brackish water, here's what the USGS guidance says you need right at the truck:

**Ambient barometric pressure, measured at your actual altitude.** The pressure "must be determined to the nearest 1 millimeter (mm) of mercury," and it is "required that the barometric pressure be measured at the altitude of the DO calibration or check" 【12】. Sea-level-adjusted weather-station readings won't do — NWS pressure "typically is adjusted to sea level... and must be adjusted back to the altitude of the weather station in order to obtain ambient barometric pressure values" 【14】. Also check the barometer's accuracy "before each field trip or at least annually" 【12】.

**Temperature stability.** Keep the calibration assembly "in a stable temperature environment and out of direct sunlight" 【5】, and allow "5 to 10 minutes for the air to saturate with water vapor and for the DO sensor and the air inside the calibration chamber to equilibrate" 【5】. Read the temperature "to the nearest 0.1 degree Celsius" 【5】.

**Salinity correction for the brackish water.** Oxygen solubility decreases as salinity increases 【3】. If your pod's multiparameter instrument has a calibrated conductivity sensor, "salinity correction to the DO concentration reading is performed automatically" 【12】. If not, you must apply a manual correction — for example, a measurement of 7.50 mg/L with a correction factor of 0.9733 is reported as 7.30 mg/L 【13】. Note that "when a manual salinity correction is made by the user during calibration, the instrument requires recalibration for each measured field variation in salinity" 【12】.

**Verification before deployment.** Confirm the reading is "within ±0.2 mg/L or 2 percent of the computed saturation value" 【5】, and record the calibration in the instrument log book 【6】.

The solubility of oxygen in water depends on the
temperature and ionic strength of the water. The higher the
atmospheric pressure on the water’s surface and the lower the
temperature and conductivity of the water, the more oxygen

physical, and biological reactions can cause the DO concentra-

after sample collection, especially if the water sampled was
originally isolated from the atmosphere as in the case of
groundwater or water in a deep lake or reservoir.

increases. Correction factors for salinity typically are applied
after measuring DO for single-point samples; however, for

For an air calibration to carry over into brackish water, here's what the USGS guidance says you need right at the truck:

**Ambient barometric pressure, measured at your actual altitude.** The pressure "must be determined to the nearest 1 millimeter (mm) of mercury," and it is "required that the barometric pressure be measured at the altitude of the DO calibration or check" 【12】. Sea-level-adjusted weather-station readings won't do — NWS pressure "typically is adjusted to sea level... and must be adjusted back to the altitude of the weather station in order to obtain ambient barometric pressure values" 【14】. Also check the barometer's accuracy "before each field trip or at least annually" 【12】.

**Temperature stability.** Keep the calibration assembly "in a stable temperature environment and out of direct sunlight" 【5】, and allow "5 to 10 minutes for the air to saturate with water vapor and for the DO sensor and the air inside the calibration chamber to equilibrate" 【5】. Read the temperature "to the nearest 0.1 degree Celsius" 【5】.

**Salinity correction for the brackish water.** Oxygen solubility decreases as salinity increases 【3】. If your pod's multiparameter instrument has a calibrated conductivity sensor, "salinity correction to the DO concentration reading is performed automatically" 【12】. If not, you must apply a manual correction — for example, a measurement of 7.50 mg/L with a correction factor of 0.9733 is reported as 7.30 mg/L 【13】. Note that "when a manual salinity correction is made by the user during calibration, the instrument requires recalibration for each measured field variation in salinity" 【12】.

**Verification before deployment.** Confirm the reading is "within ±0.2 mg/L or 2 percent of the computed saturation value" 【5】, and record the calibration in the instrument log book 【6】.

turns.question: The contract we're working under says follow the EPA field SOP, not the USGS one. Does that change how often I calibrate and what I do at the end of the day?
turns.answer:
Yes — the EPA Region 1 SOP sets its own frequency and end-of-day requirements:

**Calibration frequency.** "At a minimum, the instrument is calibrated prior to use on the day the measurements are to be performed" 【3】. Some projects may require more frequent checks during the day, and if the instrument drifted out of calibration it can be recalibrated mid-day, with only the data measured prior to that check needing qualification 【3】. For instruments that monitor continuously, they "are calibrated before deployment" and the calibration is checked when recovered 【3】. Also note some instruments lose their calibration criteria when turned off — those can be left on all day or calibrated at each sampling location 【3】.

**End of day.** "A post calibration check at the end of the day is performed to determine if the instrument drifted out of calibration" 【3】.

**What the post-check must meet.** The post-calibration value is compared against the oxygen-solubility chart, and "if measurement value drifted outside the criteria, the data will need to be qualified" 【2】. If your project plan doesn't list drift criteria, the SOP's defaults are: dissolved oxygen ±0.5 mg/L of the saturation value (or <0.5 mg/L for the 0 mg/L solution, but not a negative value), specific conductance ±5% of standard or ±10 µS/cm (whichever is greater), pH ±0.3 pH unit with pH 7 buffer, turbidity ±5% of standard, and ORP ±10 mV 【2】.

**Records.** All calibration records must be documented in the project's log book or on a calibration log sheet, including at minimum the manufacturer, model, instrument ID, standards used (with source), calibration date, instrument readings, the post-calibration check, and the name of the person(s) who performed the calibration 【2】.

2.3 Measurement
The solubility of oxygen in water depends on the
temperature and ionic strength of the water. The higher the
atmospheric pressure on the water’s surface and the lower the
temperature and conductivity of the water, the more oxygen
will be dissolved in the water.
Degassing, mineral precipitation, and other chemical,
physical, and biological reactions can cause the DO concentra-
tion of a water sample to change substantially within minutes
after sample collection, especially if the water sampled was
originally isolated from the atmosphere as in the case of
groundwater or water in a deep lake or reservoir.
The solubility of oxygen in water decreases as salinity
increases. Correction factors for salinity typically are applied
after measuring DO for single-point samples; however, for
DO measurements made with multiparameter instruments
that include calibrated specific-conductance sensors, it is
wise to activate the instrument’s internal salinity correction
algorithms. Information that pertains to oxygen solubility and
salinity is given in section 5.0, including the link to an online
program that generates tables of DO solubility values and
(or) salinity correction factors over a range of user-specified
temperature, atmospheric pressure, and salinity or specific
conductance (https://water.usgs.gov/software/DOTABLES/).

Yes — the EPA Region 1 SOP sets its own frequency and end-of-day requirements:

**Calibration frequency.** "At a minimum, the instrument is calibrated prior to use on the day the measurements are to be performed" 【3】. Some projects may require more frequent checks during the day, and if the instrument drifted out of calibration it can be recalibrated mid-day, with only the data measured prior to that check needing qualification 【3】. For instruments that monitor continuously, they "are calibrated before deployment" and the calibration is checked when recovered 【3】. Also note some instruments lose their calibration criteria when turned off — those can be left on all day or calibrated at each sampling location 【3】.

**End of day.** "A post calibration check at the end of the day is performed to determine if the instrument drifted out of calibration" 【3】.

**What the post-check must meet.** The post-calibration value is compared against the oxygen-solubility chart, and "if measurement value drifted outside the criteria, the data will need to be qualified" 【2】. If your project plan doesn't list drift criteria, the SOP's defaults are: dissolved oxygen ±0.5 mg/L of the saturation value (or <0.5 mg/L for the 0 mg/L solution, but not a negative value), specific conductance ±5% of standard or ±10 µS/cm (whichever is greater), pH ±0.3 pH unit with pH 7 buffer, turbidity ±5% of standard, and ORP ±10 mV 【2】.

**Records.** All calibration records must be documented in the project's log book or on a calibration log sheet, including at minimum the manufacturer, model, instrument ID, standards used (with source), calibration date, instrument readings, the post-calibration check, and the name of the person(s) who performed the calibration 【2】.
